auxiliary_material: The study provides extensive mechanistic context and contradictory evidence regarding metabolite levels. It details that SCFAs enhance immunotherapy efficacy via HDAC inhibition, GPR signaling, and mTOR pathway regulation, promoting CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity and cytokine production (IFN-γ, TNF-α) [65, 66, 67, 32]. However, it highlights a critical contradiction: high serum butyrate and propionate were negatively correlated with ICI efficacy in patients treated with anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab), and butyrate reduced CTLA-4 blockade efficacy in mouse models by inhibiting memory T cell accumulation and increasing Tregs [35]. Regarding Inosine, the study describes its mechanism in enhancing anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-L1 efficacy in mouse models via A2aR-cAMP-CREB signaling and Th1 differentiation, noting this effect is dependent on exogenous IFN-γ and CpG presence [72, 36]. For TMAO, the mechanism involves activating PERK-mediated ER stress and Gasdermin-E mediated pyroptosis to enhance CD8+ T cell immunity [37]. The review also lists other metabolites like Indoles (suppressing immunity via AhR in some contexts, promoting IL-22 in others) and Secondary Bile Acids (suppressing Th17 via ROR-γt inhibition) [39, 41, 44, 51].
outline_action: Identify the specific reference numbers cited in the text for the clinical cohorts (e.g., [29], [34], [37], [52]) and locate the original full-text papers to extract the precise quantitative concentration data (μM/ng/mL) for the reported metabolites in serum or TME samples. Verify if any of these studies measured intratumoral metabolite levels directly. If the original texts do not contain TME-specific quantification, note that only serum/fecal correlations are available.
remaining_gap: The gap requires quantitative physiological concentrations (e.g., μM, ng/mL) of key metabolites specifically within human *tumour microenvironments* (TME) or paired serum linked to ICI response. While the provided text cites clinical studies measuring fecal and serum/plasma metabolites (SCFAs, TMAO, Hippuric acid combinations), it does not provide specific numerical concentration values (e.g., exact μM or ng/mL thresholds) from these cohorts, nor does it report measurements directly from the human tumour microenvironment tissue itself. The concentration data mentioned ('>100 mM') refers to gut luminal accumulation based on diet, not systemic or intratumoral levels in the clinical cohorts cited.
useful_material: The study reports clinical cohort data linking fecal Short-Chain Fatty Acid (SCFA) concentrations to Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor (ICI) outcomes. Specifically, in a cohort of 52 solid tumor patients receiving anti-PD-1 therapy (nivolumab or pembrolizumab), higher fecal concentrations of acetate, propionate, butyrate, and valerate were significantly associated with longer progression-free survival [29]. Additionally, in a smaller cohort of 11 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients receiving second-line nivolumab, gut microbial metabolites including propionate and butyrate were significantly associated with long-term beneficial effects [34]. The study also notes that serum TMAO concentrations were positively correlated with progression-free survival and ICI response in clinical data [37], and a combination of plasma metabolites (hippuric acid, butyrylcarnitine, cysteine, glutathione disulfide) showed high accuracy for predicting PD-1 blockade response in NSCLC patients [52].
